backend-stack-selection.name: backend-stack-selection
backend-stack-selection.description: Use when a project needs a custom backend — deciding language, web framework, API style, architecture pattern, database, ORM, auth mechanism, and background-job approach. Each is a real, bounded 2026 option set with tradeoffs and a stated default, not an open question. Not for the frontend's own client-side auth pattern (frontend-auth) or whether a frontend needs a backend at all (stack-selection routes here once it does).
backend-stack-selection.default: — the project's own frontend is already TypeScript, or the team's own fluency is in JS/TS |

backend-testing.name: backend-testing
backend-testing.description: Use when deciding what to test and how in a backend project — unit tests for service logic vs. integration tests through the real router/validation chain. Not frontend component/e2e testing (frontend-testing) or deciding the stack itself (backend-stack-selection).
backend-testing.default: unit-test the service layer, integration-test through the router

frontend-accessibility.name: frontend-accessibility
frontend-accessibility.description: Use when building or reviewing any frontend UI for accessibility — keyboard navigation, screen-reader semantics (aria-*, roles), focus management, color contrast, motion, alt text. Not about styling mechanics or component file structure (frontend-web-styles, frontend-component-structure). Applies to every interactive component, not just forms.

frontend-analytics.name: frontend-analytics
frontend-analytics.description: Use when a project needs to measure usage, conversion, or retention — tool choice, the cookie-consent consequence of that choice, and event naming. Not for error/performance monitoring (frontend-monitoring) or feature-flag targeting data (frontend-feature-flags), even though some tools do all three.
frontend-analytics.default: a privacy-first, cookie-less tool over Google Analytics

frontend-auth.name: frontend-auth
frontend-auth.description: Use when building or reviewing the client-side side of authentication — where the session lives, protected-route/redirect flow, and logout. Not the server-side auth mechanism itself (project-profile.md's Backend → Auth row covers session-based/JWT/OAuth2/SSO) and not the XSS boundary in general (frontend-security), though this skill leans on it directly.

frontend-component-structure.name: frontend-component-structure
frontend-component-structure.description: Use when deciding how a frontend project's files are organized — Feature-Sliced Design's layers and slices (the framework default), each slice's public-API barrel (index.ts), which files are internal, component/file naming. Not about styling mechanics (CSS Modules, tokens — that's frontend-web-styles) or picking a platform (stack-selection). Applies whenever a new slice is created, an existing one is reorganized, or a project is scaffolded.

frontend-component-workshop.name: frontend-component-workshop
frontend-component-workshop.description: Use when deciding whether a project needs an isolated component dev/documentation environment (Storybook or similar), setting one up, or adding visual regression testing to it. Not about which components are shared (frontend-design-system) or component file structure (frontend-component-structure).

frontend-design-system.name: frontend-design-system
frontend-design-system.description: Use when deciding whether a component should move from feature-local to a shared design-system tier, where shared components live, or how to shape a shared component's variant API. Not about design tokens themselves (frontend-styling-concept) or Storybook/component-workshop tooling (frontend-component-workshop) — this is the promotion rule and the API shape for what's promoted.
frontend-design-system.default: — matches frontend-styling-concept's actual recorded default (CSS Modules), not a second, conflicting styling system |

frontend-feature-flags.name: frontend-feature-flags
frontend-feature-flags.description: Use when a project needs to ship behind a flag, run an A/B test, or have a kill switch for a feature — whether a tool is needed at all, and which one. Not for analytics in general (frontend-analytics), even though some tools combine both.
frontend-feature-flags.default: a hand-rolled flag, not a service, until the need outgrows it

frontend-forms.name: frontend-forms
frontend-forms.description: Use when building or reviewing a form — validation library choice, client/server validation split, error display, and double-submit prevention. Not about a specific field's accessibility semantics beyond error association (frontend-accessibility covers labels/roles generally) or the auth login form specifically (frontend-auth).

frontend-i18n.name: frontend-i18n
frontend-i18n.description: Use when a project needs more than one UI language, or when deciding whether it does — translation library choice, string extraction, pluralization, locale-aware formatting. Not about RTL layout mechanics or translating backend/email content.

frontend-monitoring.name: frontend-monitoring
frontend-monitoring.description: Use when a project ships to real users and needs client-side errors/performance reported somewhere, not just caught and hidden — tool setup, source maps, and PII scrubbing. Not the error boundary/fallback UI itself (frontend-resilience already covers that) — this is what happens to the error after it's caught.
frontend-monitoring.default: Sentry, wired into the error boundary already in place

frontend-motion.name: frontend-motion
frontend-motion.description: Use when adding or reviewing UI animation/transitions — duration/easing tokens, picking CSS vs. an animation library, page-transition vs. component-transition mechanics. Not the prefers-reduced-motion opt-out itself (frontend-accessibility already covers it) or token naming in general (frontend-styling-concept).

frontend-performance.name: frontend-performance
frontend-performance.description: Use when adding a dependency, a heavy visual feature (map, 3D, chart, animation-heavy view), or a new route — anything that can grow the bundle or slow first render. Not about CI build speed or backend latency.

frontend-resilience.name: frontend-resilience
frontend-resilience.description: Use when a component renders data that can be missing, slow to arrive, or capable of throwing during render — error boundaries, loading states, empty states. Not about network-request retry logic or backend error codes.

frontend-routing.name: frontend-routing
frontend-routing.description: Use when deciding whether a frontend needs a router library at all, picking one when it does, or handling the accessibility/performance side-effects of a route change (focus, title, scroll, code-splitting). Not for a meta-framework's own built-in router (Next.js, Remix, Astro already decide this) or for in-component focus management unrelated to navigation (frontend-accessibility).

frontend-security.name: frontend-security
frontend-security.description: Use when rendering any HTML that isn't written by hand into JSX — dangerouslySetInnerHTML, a markdown/rich-text renderer, a user-supplied URL used as href/src. Not about backend auth, secrets in commits (repo-cleanup), or CSP/headers at the infra layer.

frontend-seo.name: frontend-seo
frontend-seo.description: Use when a project has pages meant to be publicly indexed or shared (not just an authenticated app shell) — per-route meta tags, Open Graph, canonical URLs, structured data, and whether the rendering strategy even lets crawlers see them. Not for an app with no public, indexable pages.

frontend-stack-selection.name: frontend-stack-selection
frontend-stack-selection.description: Use when choosing the actual frontend technologies for a new project — UI framework, meta-framework, bundler, package manager, state management, data fetching. Each is a real, bounded set of 2026 options with tradeoffs, not an open-ended question; this skill gives the option matrix, a recommendation, and when to deviate. Not application-type/language (stack-selection, tier 0) or an already-running project's own existing choice (read its project-profile.md instead).

frontend-styling-concept.name: frontend-styling-concept
frontend-styling-concept.description: Use when deciding or documenting the cross-platform styling architecture for a project — how design tokens flow between web, Electron/Tauri, React Native, or another native UI engine, or when starting a new frontend codebase's style layer from scratch. Not for day-to-day component styling inside an already-set-up web project — that is frontend-web-styles. Not for backend/API/database work.

frontend-testing.name: frontend-testing
frontend-testing.description: Use when deciding what to test and how in a frontend project — unit tests vs end-to-end, whether to render a component in isolation, test naming/describe-block style. Not about styling or module structure (frontend-web-styles, frontend-component-structure). Applies whenever writing a new test file or deciding a feature needs test coverage.
frontend-testing.default: extract logic, test the function; cover behavior with e2e

frontend-theming.name: frontend-theming
frontend-theming.description: Use when a project needs a light/dark toggle or multiple brand themes — the switching mechanism, not the token names themselves. Not about naming tokens (frontend-styling-concept, which this skill assumes is already followed) or the prefers-reduced-motion opt-out (frontend-accessibility).
frontend-theming.default: CSS light-dark() + color-scheme, not duplicated token sets

project-profile.name: project-profile
project-profile.description: Use when connecting an existing project, creating a brand-new one, or whenever the full picture of a project (stack, platforms, infra, workflow) is needed — maintain the one project-profile table. Not for day-to-day coding tasks on an already-profiled project; read the existing profile instead of re-deriving it.

repo-ci.name: repo-ci
repo-ci.description: Use when setting up or reviewing a project's general CI pipeline — provider choice, stage order, caching, and workflow-security basics. Not the release-triggering workflow specifically (repo-release, which is additive on top of this) or the pre-commit hook (repo-lint-format).

repo-commit.name: repo-commit
repo-commit.description: Follow murpiano-dx Git rules for task branches, Conventional Commits, project Git linter settings, pull requests, and merges.
repo-commit.default: — matches this framework's own GitHub-flow default (short-lived task branches, one coherent change per PR) |

repo-containerization.name: repo-containerization
repo-containerization.description: Use when deciding whether a project needs Docker/docker-compose at all, or setting one up once it does. Not for a deploy target that doesn't need it (static hosting, a managed platform that builds from source directly).

repo-dependency-security.name: repo-dependency-security
repo-dependency-security.description: Use when setting up or reviewing automated dependency-vulnerability scanning and update automation (npm audit, Dependabot, Renovate) for a project.

repo-hosting.name: repo-hosting
repo-hosting.description: Use when deciding where a project is hosted, how many environments it needs, how secrets are managed, and whether a compliance framework applies. Each is a real option set with tradeoffs and a default — not a question to leave to the owner unprompted. Not CI/CD pipeline stages (repo-ci) or containerization itself (repo-containerization).
repo-hosting.default: — a managed-platform deployment (this skill's own Hosting default) already gets this for free, nothing to configure |

repo-init.name: repo-init
repo-init.description: Initialize a project with murpiano-dx on request, offer a GitHub origin and Git linter, remember decisions, and resume setup.

repo-lint-format.name: repo-lint-format
repo-lint-format.description: Use when setting up or reviewing a project's linter, formatter, and pre-commit hook for them — tool choice per language and what runs locally (fast, staged-files-only) vs. in CI (the full, authoritative check). Not the commit-message/agent-trace hook (repo-cleanup) or the CI workflow structure itself (repo-ci).

repo-readme.name: repo-readme
repo-readme.description: Use when writing, reviewing, or updating a repository README, GitHub description, website, topics, or badges.
repo-readme.default: — a project with nothing specific pushing toward a stronger license |

repo-release.name: repo-release
repo-release.description: Use when managing releases, tests, CI, release notes, or release automation.
repo-release.default: — any project with real external consumers (an npm package, a library, an API with a client), which this framework assumes by default |

repo-tracking.name: repo-tracking
repo-tracking.description: Use when deciding how a project tracks issues, bugs, and feature work — a dedicated tracker vs. a plain file, and how tightly it ties to commits/PRs. Not this framework's own BACKLOG.md pattern specifically (that's a worked example of the "no team" row below) or PR requirements themselves (repo-commit).

stack-selection.name: stack-selection
stack-selection.description: Use when starting a brand-new application from scratch, before any code exists — deciding the application type (web, Electron/Tauri desktop, native desktop, native/cross-platform mobile, backend service, ...) and its language/framework, then routing to the matching domain's skills. Not for adding a feature to a project whose stack is already chosen — read that domain's own skills instead (e.g. frontend-styling-concept for an existing frontend).
